content:
<Rep. Frank Pallone, Jr.>: We oppose H.R. 6409, the ``Foreign Emissions and Nonattainment Clarification for Economic Stability (FENCES) Act,'' which seeks to amend the Clean Air Act (CAA) to allow states to ignore international pollution and remove the ability of the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) to impose sanctions on states that fail to make progress toward reducing air pollution. The bill would give states that are not even trying to improve air quality a free pass, without any incentive to fix the problem. States are already not penalized for pollution they cannot control--like pollution from foreign sources or other states--so the CAA changes proposed by this bill are completely unnecessary.
BACKROUND
The Clean Air Act (CAA) is one of the most successful public health laws in U.S. history because it has delivered significant environmental and health benefits while fostering innovation and economic development. When enacting the CAA Congress recognized that there may be circumstances that worsen air quality, at no fault of the states. That is why the CAA gives EPA flexibility to work with states experiencing elevated levels of pollution from sources outside of their control, to ensure that exposure is limited and that states can grow their economies.
SUMMARY OF THE FENCES ACT
The FENCES Act is a misguided attempt to prevent states from being held accountable for poor air quality, if they also happen to experience pollution that originated internationally.
Section 2(a) and (b) of H.R. 6409 amend CAA Section 179B and adds a new CAA Section 179B(e) that would require EPA to ignore international emissions when determining whether an area is in attainment with the National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS). If areas experience any transboundary pollution, the bill would force EPA to designate these areas with poor air quality as in attainment, even when pollution levels exceed what the standard says is safe to breathe. The majority claims this provision would prevent states from being punished for emissions that they did not cause. However, the CAA already includes pathways for states to exclude pollution that originated internationally from the NAAQS accounting process. Therefore, this provision is not needed.
Furthermore, as heard in witness testimony, requiring EPA to artificially classify areas with pollution levels exceeding the NAAQS as in attainment would block the state from issuing permits for new facilities in that area. The CAA requires new sources to show their activities will not drive an area with safe levels of pollution into nonattainment. If this bill were signed into law, every new source--no matter how well controlled--would exacerbate an area's actual poor air quality, and would be unable to secure a permit.\1\ This would actively harm states and their economic growth. On the other hand, states can and do approve preconstruction permits for facilities in nonattainment areas, provided they use advanced controls and emissions offsets to improve air quality. These requirements do not exist to punish states, but rather to ensure that the health of the American public is protected. This is just one example of how the CAA balances the need to protect public health and sustain economic growth.
\1\House Committee on Energy and Commerce, Testimony of John D. Walke, Federal Clean Air Director, Natural Resources Defense Council, Hearing on Short-Circuiting Progress: How the Clean Air Act Impacts Building Necessary Infrastructure and Onshoring American Innovation, 119th Cong. (June 11, 2025); House Committee on Energy and Commerce, Testimony of Ali Mirzakhalili, Air Quality Division Administrator, Oregon Department of Environmental Quality, Hearing on From Gridlock to Growth: Permitting Reform Under the Clean Air Act, 119th Cong. (Sept. 16, 2025).
Section 2(c) adds a new CAA Section 179C to give areas in severe or extreme nonattainment for ozone or particulate matter (PM) a free pass on pollution that comes from outside the state, from exceptional events, and mobile sources that are beyond their regulatory control. The section waives sanctions and fees for states, giving those that are not even trying to improve air quality a dangerously broad exemption from accountability without any incentive to fix the problem. By including ``emissions from outside the nonattainment area'' on this list, a state could be exempted from all fees and sanctions for failing to meet CAA requirements due to pollution originating within the same state, which would be controlled by the same air regulators. This provision is a gift to polluters at the cost of public health.
CONCLUSION
H.R. 6409 would harm public health, while actively hampering American innovation. The FENCES Act would cause complete permitting gridlock in areas with pollution that exceed an air quality standard. It will also allow states to knowingly violate air quality standards without any consequences or incentives to remedy the problem. This will make Americans sicker and harm our economy thanks to increases in lost workdays and school absences. With H.R. 6409, House Republicans are trying to use accounting gimmicks to make areas with poor air quality appear much better to benefit corporate polluters, at the expense of the health of Americans across the country.
For these reasons, we opposed H.R. 6409.
Frank Pallone, Jr.,
Ranking Member.
